abstract: This article presents TubeStats and TokStats, two publicly available dashboard-based research tools that provide platform-wide statistics for YouTube and TikTok derived from genuinely random samples of their content. Because neither platform offers adequate mechanisms to produce representative samples—and access has narrowed in the 'post-API age'—researchers typically rely on opportunistic, popularity-biased samples. The authors describe the random sampling pipelines, system architecture, use cases, and the technical, financial, and ethical challenges of maintaining such open research infrastructure.
key_claims: Neither YouTube nor TikTok provides adequate sanctioned mechanisms to produce representative samples of hosted content, forcing researchers into non-generalizable opportunistic samples.
Random sampling of these platforms is feasible by exploiting their unique video ID/URL indexing schemes, without relying on restrictive research APIs.
Aggregate statistics from random samples address 'denominator problems' and 'distribution problems' by giving researchers defensible baselines to contextualize narrower, non-representative samples.
Popularity- or keyword-based samples systematically oversample algorithmically amplified content and misrepresent typical uploader behavior, especially quotidian and 'publicly private' uses.
Unpermissioned, platform-centered random sampling can be conducted ethically and is often the only route to public-interest transparency data, provided privacy safeguards are in place.
Platform use patterns differ substantially across languages and regions, so claims from one culture cannot be generalized to a platform as a whole.
methods: YouTube: 'dialing for videos'—querying purely random 11-character IDs to build a true random sample—validated against the more efficient 'random prefix sampling' method (Zhou et al., 2011) that exploits hyphenated IDs being searchable by prefix; searching via the Innertube Python package and downloading metadata/audio with yt-dlp.
YouTube language identification via OpenAI's Whisper multilingual model on audio, which is then immediately discarded (no audio/video archived).

TikTok: exploiting 64-bit binary structure of 19-digit IDs where the first 32 bits encode a Unix creation timestamp; selecting a random second, generating tens of thousands of candidate IDs for the remaining bits, and querying via Selenium to detect extant videos.

System implementation: SvelteKit front-end, static JSON summary data hosted in an S3 bucket, Chart.js for logarithmic distribution charts and percentile calculators, pandas for binning and summary-statistic generation.

Data governance: aggregate-only public dashboards, plus planned dual dataset release (a fully public de-identified CSV and a restricted full sample available to researchers upon application and agreement to privacy terms).
Collaboration with qualitative and culturally-situated researchers to follow up on metadata patterns identified in quantitative samples.
findings: Random prefix sampling produces results sufficiently similar to the slower true-random 'dialing for videos' method, justifying its use for efficiency.
Hindi YouTube differs markedly from English, Spanish, and Russian YouTube—videos are newer, shorter, more often education/entertainment, with a distinct like-to-view pattern.
Most TikTok videos are not uploaded from the US; popularity has shifted from India (late 2010s) to other Asian countries, not the US or Europe.

TubeStats percentile tools reveal how skewed engagement is—for example, a video with 150 views sits in the 68th percentile of all YouTube videos, and videos with 1,000–10,000 views fall in the top 10%.
TikTok sample generation takes on the order of months versus a few hours for YouTube, limiting update frequency.
Independent auditing cited shows TikTok's 'random' Research API is temporally biased (over 55% of returned videos posted on Saturdays), motivating alternative sampling.

Platforms are becoming increasingly hostile to automated queries (e.g., YouTube's shift from DASH to the session-oriented SABR streaming protocol), partly attributed to for-profit AI scraping, complicating maintenance.
contributions: Two open, regularly updated, publicly accessible research tools (TubeStats, live; TokStats, planned mid/late 2026) with open-source sampling and front-end code on GitHub.
Validated, reproducible random sampling methods for two major video platforms that do not depend on sanctioned APIs.
Defensible denominators and engagement distribution baselines that let other researchers contextualize non-representative samples and enable cross-platform comparison.
A privacy-preserving data-sharing model combining aggregate dashboards with paired public (de-identified) and gated full datasets.
Documented downstream use by scholars, journalists (BBC, Washington Post), and in DSA-linked moderation-workforce research, demonstrating practical value.
A candid account of the technical, financial, and ethical challenges of sustaining open research infrastructure.
framing: The work is positioned within platform studies, infrastructure studies, and the open-science-in-communication movement, responding directly to the 'APIcalypse' and 'post-API age' constraints on platform data access. It frames representative random sampling as a public-interest transparency and accountability practice, engaging debates over denominator/distribution problems, data disclosure regulation (e.g., the EU DSA), and the ethics of unpermissioned platform-centered research.
